message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after you notify the landlord. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually no more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry. | | **Entry by Landlord** | • The landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) if you suspect discrimination. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days for non‑payment) or a **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days for lease violations).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction action in court. | • Respond promptly to notices; negotiate or seek mediation if possible. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you keep receipts and notify the landlord. | • Document the defect, get a repair estimate, and keep receipts. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for damages, recover unpaid rent, or seek a declaratory judgment.
• Small claims court can handle disputes up to $20,000. | • File a claim in the appropriate county court. | | **Fair Housing** | • The Texas Fair Housing Act protects against discrimination in housing. | • File a complaint with TCHR or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | #### Quick Tips 1. **Keep Records** – Lease agreements, move‑in/move‑out inspection reports, receipts, emails, and written notices are your best evidence. 2. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, use email or certified mail so you have a paper trail. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Notice periods and deadlines are strict; missing a deadline can weaken your case. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Many counties offer free or low‑cost mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 5. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. If you’re facing a specific issue (e.g., a dispute over a security deposit, a repair that hasn’t been addressed, or a potential eviction notice), let me know the details and I can help you draft a letter or outline next steps.
